items.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011
items.q: I have to tell you that my graduate school... was playing with you and Rick [Montalbano] and Dolores [Mancuso]... On that gig at The Beeches.

ctx.x: I love those behind-the-scenes stories. And some of those skills, I mean I was thinking about the way you and I learned music, with our ear to the radio or to the record player, and these copyists doing that stuff. I will now sound old-fashioned, but those ways of learning are not around anymore that much.

No. And it’s too bad because people are losing a valuable skill. I teach guitar, and a lot of my students, if they want to learn a tune they go to the Internet and they download a tab [tablature], all right? So the music is not all music, but just numbers. But anyway, they listen to it, they see the numbers and they do that. And then they don’t really develop any kind of ear, any kind of relative pitch, so they can’t figure stuff out on their own, and then they say “I don’t need to I can get the tab.” And if it…

really don’t know which way is up, which way is down. So we say “try singing the note when you’re playing it.” Okay. So they’ll play and sing the first note and then “what’s the next note?” and you make them sing it, and now where is that, it’s over here. And so by doing this they start to sing what they play. And this goes back to another war story, which is when I first discovered that was a good way to develop the brain-instrument relationship so you’re really playing what you’re hearing not just what you…
